aiExplanation: This is the **brute-force** approach: the class simply keeps every number that was ever added in a plain array called `list`, so `add` is just a `push`. When `getProduct(k)` is called, it starts with `res = 1` and walks **backwards** from the last element over the final `k` entries, multiplying each one into `res`, then returns the result. It is easy to understand and always correct, but each query costs **O(k)** time because it re-multiplies the numbers from scratch on every call, which is why it ran slowly on the large test cases.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This version uses **prefix products** so that every query runs in constant time. Instead of storing the raw numbers, `list` stores the **running product** of everything added since the last zero, and `prod` holds the current value of that running product. Adding a non-zero number multiplies it into `prod` and pushes the new total; adding a `0` **wipes everything** by resetting `list` to an empty array and `prod` to `1`, because any product that includes that zero must be zero. In `getProduct(k)`, if fewer than `k` numbers have been added since the last zero, the window must contain that zero, so it returns `0`; if exactly `k` numbers have been added, the answer is simply `prod`; otherwise it **divides** the latest running product by the running product from `k` positions earlier, which cancels out all the earlier factors and leaves just the product of the last `k` numbers.

aiExplanation: This is another **prefix-product** approach, but it keeps a sentinel `1` at the front of `nums` so the array never needs to be cleared. Each non-zero `add` pushes the previous running product multiplied by the new number, and a `0` pushes a fresh `1` to **restart the chain** (the zero itself is never stored, so the `=== 0` check inside `add` can never actually trigger). The counter `lastZero` is meant to track how many entries sit after the most recent zero, and `getProduct(k)` returns `0` whenever `k >= lastZero` because the window would reach back into the zero; otherwise it divides the latest running product by the one `k` positions back. The bug is the initial value `lastZero = -1`: after the very first non-zero `add` it becomes `0`, so a query like `getProduct(1)` sees `1 >= 0` and wrongly returns `0` even though no zero was ever added, which is why this submission **failed**.

aiExplanation: This is the **fixed version** of the previous attempt, using the same prefix-product idea with a sentinel `1` at the front of `nums`. Every non-zero `add` pushes the previous running product times the new number, while a `0` pushes a fresh `1` so the chain restarts without clearing the array. The key change is that `lastZero` now starts at `1` and counts **the sentinel plus every number added since the last zero**, so when `k >= lastZero` the requested window necessarily reaches past the restart point into a zero and the method returns `0`; otherwise it **divides** the latest running product by the entry `k` positions earlier, which cancels the older factors and yields exactly the product of the last `k` numbers in **O(1)** time. The `=== 0` branch inside `add` is dead code since zeros are never stored, but it is harmless.
